docs.title: Wally
docs.text:
Wally is a bounded, lock-free, zero-allocation single-producer/single-consumer (SPSC) ring buffer for the JVM, built on the Foreign Function & Memory API.

One thread writes variable-length messages into an off-heap ring; one other thread reads them in order. There are no locks, no CAS loops, and no objects created per message.

flowchart LR
    P[Producer thread] -->|"tryClaim / write payload / commit"| R
    subgraph R[Off-heap ring]
        direction LR
        F1[frame] --> F2[frame] --> F3[frame ...]
    end
    R -->|"read(handler, limit)"| C[Consumer thread]

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Off-heap memory. The ring and its two cursors live in one MemorySegment, outside the garbage-collected heap.
  • Claim, write, commit. The producer claims space for a frame, writes the payload directly into the ring, then publishes it with a single release store of the tail. The consumer reads the tail with an acquire load, so a frame it can see is always complete.
  • Variable-length frames. Each frame is an 8-byte header (length) plus the payload, padded to 8 bytes. A length of 0 marks a wrap to the start of the ring.
  • Explicit backpressure. tryClaim returns false when the ring is full; the producer decides whether to spin, drop or slow down.
  • No false sharing. The head and tail cursors are 128 bytes apart off-heap, and the writer's and reader's private state is padded on-heap.

The implementation notes cover the protocol in detail, including the wrap-sentinel ordering.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
RingBuffer ring = new RingBuffer(new RingBufferConfig().capacity(1 << 20));
Writer writer = ring.writer();   // producer thread only
Reader reader = ring.reader();   // consumer thread only

// Producer
if (writer.tryClaim(8)) {
    writer.buffer().set(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, writer.offset(), 42L);
    writer.commit();
}

// Consumer
reader.read((buf, off, len, pos) -> {
    long value = buf.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, off);
}, 100);

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: All numbers are 1P1C: one producer thread and one consumer thread running concurrently. Raw outputs are checked in under wally-bench/results/.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: CPU Apple M4 Pro, 14 cores (10 performance + 4 efficiency) Memory 24 GB OS macOS 26.4.1, no core pinning or isolation (macOS has no thread affinity API) JDK OpenJDK 25.0.5+8-LTS (Temurin), default flags; latency runs add -Xms1g -Xmx1g -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch JMH 1.37

docs.title: Throughput
docs.text:
SpscThroughputBenchmark: JMH @Group with one offer thread and one poll thread, both non-blocking, one message per call. Score is messages handed from producer to consumer per second (polled counter). 3 forks × 5 × 1 s measurement after 5 × 1 s warmup.

Queue Payload Throughput (msgs/s) ns per message Allocation (B/op) Wally RingBuffer (1 MB ring) 32-byte frame payload, written into the ring 73.5M ± 3.2M 13.6 ≈ 0 JCTools SpscArrayQueue (32K slots) preallocated object reference 399.4M ± 17.5M 2.5 ≈ 0 ArrayBlockingQueue (32K slots) preallocated object reference 19.7M ± 8.0M 50.7 2.8 ± 3.1

Wally is about 3.7x faster than ArrayBlockingQueue and about 5.4x slower than JCTools in this per-message test. The comparison is not like for like: JCTools moves a 4-byte reference and signals through the slot itself (null/non-null), so producer and consumer never write a shared cursor. Wally copies a payload and, with read(handler, 1), publishes the head cursor with a release store on every message, which moves that cache line to the consumer core and back each time. Larger read batches amortize the head store.

docs.title: Latency
docs.text:
SpscLatency: the producer offers 1M msgs/s at a fixed schedule and stamps each message with its intended send time, so stalls and full-queue waits count as latency (no coordinated omission). The consumer busy-polls and records System.nanoTime() - stamp into an HdrHistogram. 5 s warmup, then 20 s (20M messages) measured.

Queue p50 p99 p99.9 p99.99 max Wally 83 ns 458 ns 24.2 µs 737 µs 1.78 ms JCTools SpscArrayQueue 84 ns 334 ns 13.1 µs 572 µs 1.66 ms

Read these with care:

  • System.nanoTime() on Apple Silicon ticks at 24 MHz, about 42 ns per tick, so the p50 values carry ±42 ns quantization.
  • Everything above p99 is dominated by the OS scheduler on an unpinned macOS laptop. Neither number above p99 should be cited as a property of the queue.

docs.title: Allocation and correctness checks
docs.text:
• ZeroAllocationTest runs 50M write/read cycles under Epsilon GC with a 128 MB heap as part of ./gradlew check; any per-op allocation fails it with OutOfMemoryError.
  • jcstress (./gradlew :wally-stress:jcstress -Pjcstress.args="-m default"): 68/68 configurations passed for the plain and wrap-sentinel publication tests.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
./gradlew :wally-bench:jmh -Pjmh.profilers=gc   # wally-bench/results/jmh-throughput.json
./gradlew :wally-bench:latency                  # wally-bench/results/latency-*.hgrm

docs.title: Implementation Details
docs.text: This document explains the internal implementation of Wally's SPSC ring buffer, covering memory layout, algorithms, and design decisions. The reasoning behind each decision is recorded in the ADRs.

docs.title: Overall Structure
docs.text:
The ring buffer consists of two regions allocated in a single contiguous block:

Offset    Size      Description
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
0         256B      Cursor metadata (head + tail with padding)
256       N bytes   Ring buffer data (capacity)

Total allocation: 256 + capacity bytes, aligned to 64-byte boundary.

docs.title: Cursor Metadata Layout
docs.text:
Byte      Content                              Purpose
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
0-55      Padding (unused)                     Cache line padding
56-63     Head cursor (long)                   Consumer's read position
64-183    Padding (unused)                     Prevent false sharing
184-191   Tail cursor (long)                   Producer's write position
192-255   Padding (unused)                     Cache line padding

Rationale: 128-byte separation prevents false sharing even with Adjacent Cache Line Prefetch (Intel) which speculatively loads adjacent cache lines.

Virtual cursors: Both head and tail are monotonically increasing 64-bit integers representing byte offsets in a virtual infinite buffer. The actual ring index is computed via masking.

docs.title: Ring Buffer Data Layout
docs.text:
Frames are stored contiguously with wrapping at capacity boundary:

Frame structure:
┌──────────┬──────────┬────────────────────────────┐
│ Length   │ Padding  │ Payload (8-byte aligned)   │
│ 4 bytes  │ 4 bytes  │ length bytes, padded to 8  │
└──────────┴──────────┴────────────────────────────┘
◄────── 8 bytes ─────►◄──────── aligned ──────────►

Length field: Contains actual payload size (not padded size). Allows reader to deliver exact message length to handler.

Padding: 4 bytes after length ensures payload starts at 8-byte aligned offset. Required for ValueLayout operations.

Payload padding: Payload is padded to 8-byte boundary so next frame starts aligned.

docs.title: Index Calculation
docs.text:
Ring indices are computed from virtual cursors via masking:

int index = (int) (cursor & mask);

Where mask = capacity - 1 (capacity must be power of 2).

Example (capacity = 256, mask = 0xFF): 

cursor = 0     → index = 0
cursor = 100   → index = 100
cursor = 256   → index = 0    (wrap)
cursor = 300   → index = 44

Benefits: - Fast modulo via single AND operation - No branch mispredictions - Natural sequence numbers from cursor values - Avoids wrapping arithmetic complexity

docs.title: Phase 1: Claim Space
docs.text:
boolean tryClaim(int length) {
    int frameSize = HEADER_SIZE + align(length, 8);

    long tail = this.tail;                 // writer owns tail: plain field, no atomic load
    int tailIndex = (int) (tail & mask);

    if (tailIndex + frameSize > capacity) {
        // The gap [tail, nextLap) must be free before the sentinel is written,
        // otherwise the sentinel could overwrite an unread frame's length.
        long nextLap = (tail & ~mask) + capacity;
        if (!hasSpace(nextLap)) return false;          // nothing written
        data.set(JAVA_INT, tailIndex, 0);              // sentinel
        this.tail = tail = nextLap;
        tailIndex = 0;
        setLongRelease(memory, tailOffset, tail);      // publish the skip on its own
    }

    long newTail = tail + frameSize;
    if (!hasSpace(newTail)) return false;              // nothing written
    data.set(JAVA_INT, tailIndex, length);             // invisible until commit
    claimedTail = tail;
    claimedNextTail = newTail;
    return true;
}

boolean hasSpace(long newTail) {
    if (newTail - cachedHead <= capacity) return true;
    cachedHead = getLongAcquire(memory, headOffset);   // refresh only when the cached value says full
    return newTail - cachedHead <= capacity;
}

Key points: - Space check before any write: The writer never writes to ring memory it has not proven free. An earlier version wrote the sentinel first; with mixed frame sizes and a full ring that zeroed the header of an unread frame, and the reader silently skipped the rest of the lap. RingBufferWrapTest reproduces that case. - Skip published separately: A frame that must wrap needs the reader to have consumed the gap at the end of the lap. Publishing the sentinel as its own tail update lets the reader move past it, so a frame larger than both the gap and tailIndex still gets placed once the reader catches up. - Cached head: The writer only performs an acquire load of head when the cached value says the ring is full. - Uncommitted state: The length is written but the tail is not advanced, so the reader cannot see the frame.

docs.title: Phase 2: Write Payload
docs.text:
long payloadOffset = writer.offset();  // index + HEADER_SIZE, relative to writer.buffer()
writer.buffer().set(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, payloadOffset, value);

Zero-copy: buffer() is a slice of the data region (it excludes the cursors), created once at construction.

docs.title: Phase 3: Commit
docs.text:
void commit() {
    tail = claimedNextTail;
    setLongRelease(memory, tailOffset, tail);  // publish
}

Memory ordering: setLongRelease ensures all prior writes (length field, payload) are visible before the new tail value. This is the synchronization point.

docs.title: Read Algorithm
docs.text:
int read(MessageHandler handler, int limit) {
    int count = 0;
    long currentHead = head;
    long tail = cachedTail;
    try {
        while (count < limit) {
            if (currentHead >= tail) {
                tail = getLongAcquire(memory, tailOffset);  // refresh only when the cached tail is exhausted
                cachedTail = tail;
                if (currentHead >= tail) break;
            }
            int headIndex = (int) (currentHead & mask);
            int length = data.get(JAVA_INT, headIndex);
            if (length == 0) {                                // sentinel
                currentHead = (currentHead & ~mask) + capacity;
                continue;
            }
            long position = currentHead;
            currentHead += HEADER_SIZE + align(length, 8);   // advance before the callback
            handler.onMessage(data, headIndex + HEADER_SIZE, length, position);
            count++;
        }
    } finally {
        head = currentHead;
        setLongRelease(memory, headOffset, currentHead);
    }
    return count;
}

Key points: - Acquire read of tail: Synchronizes with the writer's release write, so every frame below the observed tail is fully visible. A batch reuses the observed tail and only reloads it once exhausted. - Local head: Read position kept in a local until the batch completes, then published once. - Exception safety: The finally block publishes the head even if a handler throws; the frame whose handler threw counts as consumed.

docs.title: Synchronization Protocol
docs.text: The correctness of SPSC communication relies on acquire/release ordering:

docs.title: Happens-Before Relationships
docs.text:
Producer Thread                 Consumer Thread
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Write length field
2. Write payload data
3. setLongRelease(tail) ────┐
                            │  happens-before
                            └──> 4. getLongAcquire(tail)
                                 5. Read length field
                                 6. Read payload data
                                 7. setLongRelease(head)
                            ┌──> 8. getLongAcquire(head)
                            │  happens-before
                            └────

Guarantees: - Operations 1-2 are visible after operation 4 (acquire loads preceding release store) - Consumer never sees partial writes - Consumer never reads uncommitted frames (tail not advanced)

docs.title: Implementation via VarHandle
docs.text:
private static final VarHandle LONG = ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG.varHandle();

public static long getLongAcquire(MemorySegment seg, long offset) {
    return (long) LONG.getAcquire(seg, offset);
}

public static void setLongRelease(MemorySegment seg, long offset, long value) {
    LONG.setRelease(seg, offset, value);
}

JMM Semantics (JLS §17.4): - Release write: Prevents reordering of prior writes past the release - Acquire read: Prevents reordering of subsequent reads before the acquire - Together: Establishes synchronization between threads

Hardware: On x86-64, acquire loads and release stores compile to plain MOVs (TSO already provides the ordering). On AArch64, HotSpot emits LDAR/STLR.

docs.title: Available Space Calculation
docs.text:
long availableSpace = capacity - (tail - head);

Invariant: tail - head ≤ capacity always holds.

Proof: - Initially: head = tail = 0, difference is 0 - Writer advances tail only if tail + frameSize - head ≤ capacity - Reader advances head, reducing the difference - Thus: tail - head ≤ capacity maintained

docs.title: Full vs Empty
docs.text:
// Empty
head == tail

// Full
tail - head == capacity

// Partially filled
0 < tail - head < capacity

No ambiguity between empty and full (unlike some ring buffer designs that need an extra slot or flag).

docs.title: Sentinel Placement
docs.text:
When a frame doesn't fit at the end:

Before wrap (tail = 232, capacity = 256):
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ... existing data ... │ 24 bytes free          │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                        ↑ tailIndex = 232

Need 40-byte frame → doesn't fit

The sentinel is only written once the writer has confirmed the reader already consumed [232, 256); the new tail (256) is published immediately.

After sentinel write:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ... existing data ... │ [0]│ 20 bytes unused   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                        ↑ sentinel

Virtual cursor advanced: tail = (232 & ~255) + 256 = 256
Physical index: tailIndex = 256 & 255 = 0

Frame written at index 0:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [len=32][payload...]   │ ... (old data)        │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ↑ tailIndex = 0

Virtual cursor now: tail = 256 + 40 = 296

Virtual cursor arithmetic: (cursor & ~mask) + capacity advances to next lap without changing physical index to 0 yet. Next modulo operation yields index 0.

docs.title: Reader Handling of Sentinel
docs.text:
int length = memory.get(JAVA_INT, framePos);
if (length == 0) {
    // Sentinel: advance to next lap
    currentHead = (currentHead & ~mask) + capacity;
    continue;  // Skip to next iteration
}

Reader skips sentinel without calling handler. Next frame is at physical index 0.

docs.title: Why 8-Byte Alignment?
docs.text:
1. ValueLayout requirement: JAVA_LONG, JAVA_DOUBLE require 8-byte aligned offsets
  2. Performance: Aligned access avoids crossing cache line boundaries
  3. Atomicity: Many platforms guarantee atomic access only for aligned words
  4. Simplicity: Single alignment value for all operations

docs.title: Alignment Enforcement
docs.text:
Frame alignment: 

int frameSize = HEADER_SIZE + align(payloadLength, 8);

Where align(x, 8) = (x + 7) & ~7.

Cursor start: dataOffset() returns 256, which is 8-byte aligned (256 % 8 = 0).

Virtual cursor arithmetic: Adding multiples of 8 preserves alignment.

Result: Every payload offset is 8-byte aligned: 

payloadOffset = dataOffset (256, aligned)
                + tailIndex (sum of aligned frame sizes, aligned)
                + HEADER_SIZE (8, aligned)
              = aligned

docs.title: False Sharing Prevention
docs.text:
Core 0 (Producer)                 Core 1 (Consumer)
┌─────────────────┐               ┌─────────────────┐
│   L1 Cache      │               │   L1 Cache      │
│  ┌────────┐     │               │  ┌────────┐     │
│  │  Tail  │     │               │  │  Head  │     │
│  └────────┘     │               │  └────────┘     │
└─────────────────┘               └─────────────────┘
        │                                 │
        └────────── L3 (Shared) ──────────┘
                 ┌──────────────────┐
                 │ Cache line 0:    │
                 │   Head + padding │
                 ├──────────────────┤
                 │ Cache line 2+:   │  (128B gap)
                 │   Tail + padding │
                 └──────────────────┘

Without padding: Producer writes to tail → cache line invalidation → consumer's cache line evicted → false sharing → performance degradation.

With 128B padding: Head and tail in separate cache lines (even with 128B prefetching). Cores can operate without invalidating each other's caches.

docs.title: On-Heap Writer/Reader State
docs.text: The writer's private fields (tail, claimedTail, claimedNextTail, cachedHead) and the reader's (head, cachedTail) are written on every operation by different threads. The two objects are allocated back to back, so without padding they share a cache line (JOL: 40 + 32 bytes) and undo the off-heap cursor padding. Both classes use inheritance padding: 128 bytes of long fields in a superclass, the hot fields in a middle class, and 128 bytes in the subclass, because HotSpot lays out superclass fields first. RingBufferLayoutTest asserts the result with JOL; it already caught HotSpot packing an int field into the 4-byte gap after the object header, ahead of the padding.

docs.title: Spatial Locality
docs.text:
Ring buffer data is contiguous. Sequential reads/writes benefit from: - Hardware prefetching - Cache line fills (64 bytes loaded at once) - TLB efficiency (fewer page table entries)

Optimization: Size frames to fit cache lines. Example: 56-byte payload + 8-byte header = 64 bytes = 1 cache line.

docs.title: Minimum Capacity
docs.text:
Constraint: Capacity must hold at least one maximum-size frame.

if (frameSize > capacity) {
    throw new MessageTooLargeException(length, capacity, "...");
}

Minimum sensible capacity: 64 (one cache line).

docs.title: Maximum Message Size
docs.text:
Limited by frame size fitting in ring:

maxMessageSize = capacity - HEADER_SIZE;

A frame of exactly capacity bytes can only be placed at index 0 with an empty ring, so the writer waits for the reader to drain fully first.

docs.title: Sentinel at Index 0
docs.text:
If a message ends exactly at capacity boundary, next message naturally starts at index 0. No sentinel needed.

if (tailIndex + frameSize > capacity) {  // Strictly greater
    // Write sentinel
}

Equal case (==) does not write sentinel.

docs.title: Full Ring with Sentinel
docs.text: The gap between the sentinel and the end of the lap counts as used space: the tail jumps to the next lap, so tail - head includes it until the reader skips past. No separate adjustment is needed.

docs.title: Overflow Protection
docs.text:
64-bit cursors: At 10B messages/sec, would take 58 years to overflow. No special handling needed in practice.

If overflow concerns exist: 

if (tail > Long.MAX_VALUE - frameSize) {
    // Wrap cursors back to 0 (requires coordination)
}

Wally does not implement this (not needed for realistic workloads).

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Measured numbers and methodology are in Benchmarks.

docs.title: Power-of-Two Capacity
docs.text:
Pros: - Fast modulo via AND - No division instructions - Compiler optimizes mask constant

Cons: - Wastes capacity if natural size isn't power of 2 - Example: Need 1500 KB → must allocate 2048 KB

Decision: Performance benefit outweighs waste.

docs.title: 8-Byte Header
docs.text:
Alternative: 4-byte header (length only, no padding).

Pros of 8-byte: - Payload always aligned - No conditional alignment logic - Simpler arithmetic

Cons of 8-byte: - 4 bytes overhead per message - Example: 1M × 32-byte messages → 4 MB wasted

Decision: Simplicity and alignment guarantees worth the overhead.

docs.title: Virtual Cursors
docs.text:
Alternative: Wrap cursors at capacity.

Pros of virtual cursors: - Natural sequence numbers - No wrap-around arithmetic - Simpler space calculation - Easier to reason about

Cons: - 64-bit arithmetic (negligible on 64-bit CPUs)

Decision: Virtual cursors preferred for simplicity.

docs.title: Cached Head in Writer
docs.text:
Benefit: Reduces contention on head cursor. Writer only reads when space check fails.

Cost: May claim space that was recently freed (brief full condition).

docs.title: Safety Properties
docs.text:
1. No data races: All shared memory accessed with acquire/release
  2. No lost messages: Every committed message eventually read (if capacity sufficient)
  3. FIFO order: Messages read in write order
  4. Exactly-once delivery: Each message read once (reader advances atomically)
  5. No partial reads: Consumer sees complete message (synchronization protocol)

docs.title: Liveness Properties
docs.text:
1. Bounded steps: tryClaim, commit and read never block or retry internally; a full or empty ring returns immediately.
  2. Writer progress: Any frame up to capacity bytes is eventually placed once the reader drains enough space.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• RingBufferWrapTest: deterministic reproduction of the sentinel-overwrite case, plus 2M random-size messages across two threads with per-byte payload checks
  • RingBufferTest / EdgeCaseTest: protocol, wrapping, backpressure and argument validation
  • RingBufferLayoutTest (JOL): at least 128 bytes of padding around the writer and reader hot fields
  • ZeroAllocationTest (Epsilon GC, 128 MB heap): 50M write/read cycles without allocation
  • jcstress (wally-stress): a reader that sees a non-zero length sees the full payload, with and without a wrap

docs.title: Quick Start Guide
docs.text: Get started with Wally SPSC ring buffer in 5 minutes. This guide assumes Java 22+ and basic knowledge of off-heap memory via FFM API.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Wally is not published yet (current version 0.1.0-SNAPSHOT). Use a composite build:

// settings.gradle.kts
includeBuild("../wally")

// build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation("io.wally:wally-core:0.1.0-SNAPSHOT")
}

docs.title: 1. Create a Ring Buffer
docs.text:
import io.wally.spsc.*;

RingBuffer ring = new RingBuffer(
    new RingBufferConfig()
        .capacity(1024 * 1024)  // 1 MB, must be power of 2
);

Writer writer = ring.writer();  // Use from producer thread only
Reader reader = ring.reader();  // Use from consumer thread only

docs.title: 2. Write Messages (Producer)
docs.text:
Option A: Zero-copy (fastest)

import java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout;

if (writer.tryClaim(32)) {
    var buf = writer.buffer();
    long off = writer.offset();

    // Write directly into ring
    buf.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, off, orderId);
    buf.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_DOUBLE, off + 8, price);
    buf.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, off + 16, quantity);
    buf.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_BYTE, off + 20, side);

    writer.commit();  // Make visible to consumer
}

Option B: Copy from byte array

byte[] order = serializeOrder(...);
if (!writer.write(order, 0, order.length)) {
    // Ring full - consumer needs to drain
}

docs.title: 3. Read Messages (Consumer)
docs.text:
reader.read((buf, off, len, seq) -> {
    // Parse message
    long orderId = buf.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, off);
    double price = buf.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_DOUBLE, off + 8);
    int quantity = buf.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, off + 16);

    // Process order
    executeOrder(orderId, price, quantity);
}, 100);  // Read up to 100 messages

docs.title: Complete Example: Order Flow
docs.text:
package com.example.trading;

import io.wally.spsc.*;
import java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout;

public class OrderProcessor {

    private final RingBuffer ring;
    private final Writer writer;
    private final Reader reader;

    public OrderProcessor() {
        this.ring = new RingBuffer(
            new RingBufferConfig().capacity(64 * 1024)
        );
        this.writer = ring.writer();
        this.reader = ring.reader();
    }

    // Producer thread
    public boolean sendOrder(long orderId, double price, int quantity, byte side) {
        if (!writer.tryClaim(21)) {
            return false;  // Ring full
        }

        var buf = writer.buffer();
        long off = writer.offset();
        buf.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, off, orderId);
        buf.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_DOUBLE, off + 8, price);
        buf.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, off + 16, quantity);
        buf.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_BYTE, off + 20, side);

        writer.commit();
        return true;
    }

    // Consumer thread
    public void processOrders() {
        reader.read((buf, off, len, seq) -> {
            long orderId = buf.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, off);
            double price = buf.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_DOUBLE, off + 8);
            int quantity = buf.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, off + 16);
            byte side = buf.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_BYTE, off + 20);

            System.out.printf("Order %d: %s %d @ %.2f%n",
                orderId, side == 'B' ? "BUY" : "SELL", quantity, price);
        }, 1000);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        OrderProcessor processor = new OrderProcessor();

        // Start consumer thread
        Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
            while (!Thread.interrupted()) {
                processor.processOrders();
            }
        });
        consumer.start();

        // Producer thread (main)
        for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
            while (!processor.sendOrder(
                i, 100.0 + i, 100, (byte) 'B'
            )) {
                Thread.onSpinWait();  // Busy-spin until space available
            }
        }

        Thread.sleep(100);
        consumer.interrupt();
        consumer.join();
    }
}

docs.title: Zero-Allocation Handler
docs.text:
class ReusableHandler implements MessageHandler {
    private long orderCount;

    @Override
    public void onMessage(MemorySegment buf, long off, int len, long seq) {
        orderCount++;
        // Process without allocating
    }
}

ReusableHandler handler = new ReusableHandler();
reader.read(handler, 100);  // No lambda allocation

docs.title: Backpressure Handling
docs.text:
// Option 1: Spin-wait
while (!writer.tryClaim(32)) {
    Thread.onSpinWait();
}

// Option 2: Drop message
if (!writer.tryClaim(32)) {
    droppedMessages.increment();
    return;
}

// Option 3: Batch and retry
List<Message> pending = new ArrayList<>();
for (Message msg : messages) {
    if (!write(msg)) {
        pending.add(msg);
    }
}

docs.title: Batch Processing
docs.text:
// Producer: write multiple
for (Order order : orders) {
    if (!writeOrder(order)) break;  // Stop when full
}

// Consumer: drain all
int read = reader.read(handler, Integer.MAX_VALUE);

docs.title: Performance Tips
docs.text:
1. Reuse handlers: Don't use capturing lambdas in hot path
  2. Power-of-two capacity: Enables fast modulo via masking
  3. Thread affinity: Pin producer/consumer to separate cores
  4. Warmup: Run 10K ops before measuring latency
  5. Batch reads: Read multiple messages per call

docs.title: ADR 0001: Use the FFM API instead of Unsafe
docs.text: Status: Accepted · Date: 2026-11-28

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The ring buffer lives off-heap so messages create no garbage, and its cursors need acquire/release access on raw memory. Historically that meant sun.misc.Unsafe or direct ByteBuffers.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Use the final Foreign Function & Memory API (JEP 454): one MemorySegment per ring allocated from an Arena, ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG.varHandle() for acquire/release cursor access, and plain ValueLayout accessors for frame headers and payloads. Bytecode targets Java 22 (--release 22); the build uses JDK 25.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• + Supported API: Unsafe memory access warns from JDK 24 and is slated for removal.
  • + Bounds and liveness checks that the JIT removes on hot paths.
  • + Lifetime is explicit: the default Arena.ofAuto() frees the ring when unreachable, Arena.ofShared() frees it on close().
  • − Producer and consumer are different threads, so Arena.ofConfined() cannot be used: its segments throw WrongThreadException off the owner thread.
  • − Requires Java 22+. Excludes users on 17/21.
  • − asSlice() allocates, so slicing happens once at construction and the hot-path API passes (segment, offset, length) instead of per-message slices.

docs.title: ADR 0002: Variable-length frames addressed by virtual byte cursors
docs.text: Status: Accepted · Date: 2026-11-28

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Typical payloads (orders, quotes, market-data ticks) vary in size. Fixed-size slots either waste space or cap the message size, and slot-of-references queues force a heap object per message.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Messages are stored inline as frames: an 8-byte header (4-byte length + 4 bytes padding) followed by the payload, padded so every frame is a multiple of 8 bytes. Payloads are therefore always 8-byte aligned for ValueLayout access.
  • head and tail are monotonically increasing 64-bit byte positions ("virtual cursors"). The ring index is cursor & (capacity - 1), so capacity must be a power of two.
  • A length of 0 is reserved as the wrap sentinel (ADR 0004), so zero-length messages are rejected.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• + No per-message objects; the producer writes straight into the ring (zero copy).
  • + Empty (head == tail) and full (tail - head == capacity) are unambiguous without a spare slot; 64-bit cursors do not overflow in practice.
  • − Reader.sequence() and the handler's sequence argument are byte positions, not message counts, and available() is in bytes.
  • − 8 bytes of header plus up to 7 bytes of padding per message, and a power-of-two capacity.

docs.title: ADR 0003: Claim/commit publication with acquire/release and cached cursors
docs.text: Status: Accepted · Date: 2026-11-28

docs.title: Context
docs.text: With exactly one producer and one consumer, each cursor has a single writer, so no CAS or locks are needed. What remains is making a frame visible only once it is complete, and keeping cross-core cursor traffic low.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Claim, write, commit. tryClaim(length) reserves a frame and writes its length header; the caller writes the payload in place; commit() publishes it with a single release store of tail. The consumer acquire-loads tail and only reads frames below it.
  • Owner keeps a local copy. The writer holds its own tail in a field and never re-reads it from shared memory; the reader does the same for head.
  • Cache the other side's cursor. The writer acquire-loads head only when its cached value says the ring is full; the reader acquire-loads tail only when its cached value is exhausted.
  • Non-blocking backpressure. tryClaim returns false when the ring is full and read returns 0 when it is empty. Waiting strategy (spin, yield, drop) is the caller's choice.
  • Consumption on callback. A frame counts as consumed once its handler is invoked, even if the handler throws; the head is published once per read call.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• + One release store per message on the producer side, no fences beyond acquire/release, no CAS.
  • + Every operation completes in a bounded number of steps.
  • − Single-threaded use per side is a contract the API cannot enforce.
  • − read(handler, 1) publishes head on every message, which bounces that cache line between cores. This is the main reason JCTools SpscArrayQueue is faster in the per-message throughput benchmark; larger read batches amortize it.

docs.title: ADR 0004: Write the wrap sentinel only after the gap is proven free
docs.text: Status: Accepted · Date: 2026-11-28

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Frames never straddle the end of the ring. When a frame does not fit in the remaining bytes of the current lap, the writer marks the rest of the lap as unused with a sentinel (length 0) and places the frame at index 0 of the next lap.

An earlier implementation wrote the sentinel first and checked free space afterwards. When the ring was full, the sentinel landed on the length header of an unread frame; the reader then took that frame for a wrap and silently skipped the rest of the lap. Uniform message sizes hid the bug because the overwritten header was already a sentinel.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. If the frame does not fit before the end of the lap, compute nextLap = (tail & ~mask) + capacity and check that [tail, nextLap) is free (nextLap - head <= capacity). If not, return false without writing anything.
  2. Write the sentinel, set tail = nextLap, and publish it with a release store immediately.
  3. Check space for the frame at index 0. If there is none, return false; the published skip stays valid.
  4. Write the length header only after the frame's space check succeeds.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• + The writer never writes to memory the reader has not consumed.
  • + Publishing the skip separately fixes a liveness bug: a frame larger than both the remaining gap and the current index could otherwise never be placed, because it needed the reader to pass a tail that had not moved.
  • − A wrap costs one extra release store.
  • Verified by RingBufferWrapTest (deterministic reproduction that fails on the old ordering, plus 2M random-size messages across two threads) and the jcstress SpscWrapPublishTest.

docs.title: ADR 0005: Pad both off-heap cursors and on-heap writer/reader state
docs.text: Status: Accepted · Date: 2026-11-28

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The producer writes tail and its private claim state on every message; the consumer writes head and its cached tail. If any of these share a cache line, each write invalidates the other core's copy.

Padding only the off-heap cursors is not enough. The writer and reader objects are allocated back to back (JOL: 40 and 32 bytes), so their hot fields can sit in the same heap cache line.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Off-heap: head and tail each sit in their own 128-byte block (two 64-byte lines, covering adjacent-line prefetch), followed by the data region.
  • On-heap: inheritance padding. A superclass with 16 long fields (128 bytes), a middle class with the hot fields, and a subclass with 16 more long fields. HotSpot lays out superclass fields first, so field reordering cannot move hot fields into the padding.
  • No int hot fields. HotSpot fills the 4-byte gap after the compressed object header with a small field from any class in the hierarchy, which put int claimedLength in front of the padding. The claimed length is read from the frame header instead.
  • RingBufferLayoutTest asserts with JOL that at least 128 bytes precede and follow the hot fields of both objects.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• + Producer and consumer state live in separate cache lines regardless of allocation order.
  • + The layout is checked in CI, so a JVM or field change that breaks it fails the build.
  • − About 300 bytes per writer/reader object.
  • − @Contended would be shorter but needs -XX:-RestrictContended for non-JDK code, which a library cannot require.
